teach/pre: Start with a language model that has already been trained, on a huge amount of text, to predict the next token. That is a pretrained model: its training is done before anyone puts it to work.
teach/job: Now you want it for one particular job: turning English words into French. How do you teach it that?
teach/tune: The usual way was fine-tuning: train it some more on thousands of solved examples, with a gradient step on each. That changes the weights, and every new job needs a training run of its own.
teach/continue: But a language model already does one thing well: it continues whatever text it is given. That text is called the prompt.
teach/prompt: So write the job itself into the prompt: an instruction, English to French, then a new input, cheese, and an arrow.
teach/few: Better still, first show it a few solved examples: dog becomes chien, cow becomes vache.
teach/answer: Now the likeliest continuation is fromage. No training run, no gradient step: the model picked up the task from the examples in front of it.
context/context: Everything the model can read at once is called its context: the prompt, plus anything the model has written since. Not to be confused with a context vector: this context is the text itself.
context/limit: It has room for only so many tokens. Picture it as a box of fixed size, with the prompt filling the start of it.
context/attend: The examples are tokens in that box like any others. Attention lets the last position read every token before it, and to predict what follows such a pattern, the model has to work out the task.
context/name: That is why it is called in-context learning. The task is learned from examples in the context, and the learning lives there, not in the weights.
context/brown: In 2020, Tom Brown and colleagues at Open A I described it in their paper on G P T three, a model with a hundred and seventy five billion parameters. Given a few examples in its prompt, and no gradient step, it sometimes rivaled models fine-tuned for the task.
context/shots: They sorted prompts by how many solved examples, or shots, they show. No examples is zero-shot, one is one-shot, and several, like ours, is few-shot.
frozen/pass: So what did the examples change? Copy the weights, then run the prompt. That is a forward pass: it computes no loss and no gradient, so nothing takes a step.
frozen/same: Every weight is exactly what it was. The examples changed only the context, and through attention, what the model predicts next.
frozen/gone: So nothing is kept. Send a new prompt without the examples, and the model starts from the same weights, with no trace of them.
room/parts: Examples do cost one thing: room in the context. Here the instruction takes five tokens, and the new input three.
room/each: Say each example takes six tokens. Our two take twelve.
room/total: Five, plus twelve, plus three: twenty tokens for the model to read before it answers.
room/limit: And the box has a limit. In G P T three, it held two thousand and forty eight tokens, room for between ten and a hundred examples. Say ours holds one thousand and twenty four.
room/left: The instruction and the input take eight of them, which leaves one thousand and sixteen for examples.
room/fit: At six tokens each, one thousand and sixteen over six is about a hundred and sixty nine point three.
room/down: Only whole examples fit, so round down: a hundred and sixty nine of them, taking one thousand and fourteen tokens. One more would spill past the limit.
